d.title: Five bounds, five levels of information - and the price of each
d.caption: **The bound tightens exactly as fast as you are willing to assume**, which is the whole shape of this lesson. Markov needs almost nothing and tells you almost nothing; Chernoff needs your variables to be indicators and pays fourteen orders of magnitude for it. **McDiarmid is the one that changes the kind of question you can ask**, because it drops the requirement that the quantity be an average at all — the empirical risk of a classifier concentrates by the same argument, with every constant equal to one over n.

d.title: The denominator is a sum of squares, and that is the lesson
d.caption: **The same total sensitivity concentrated in one argument is far worse than spread across many**, because the sum of squares grows linearly while a single large constant is squared on its own. Ten inputs each able to move the output by 0.1 give a near-useless 0.449; one input able to move it by 0.1 with the rest unable to move it at all gives essentially zero. **A statistic with one influential input does not concentrate**, however much data you have — a statement about leverage rather than sample size, and the reason clipping buys a guarantee rather than merely tidier numbers.

d.title: Six principles, and the door each one closes
d.caption: **Only the first makes a positive claim**; the other five are statements about what a p-value is not. Read them as a list of the inferences people draw anyway — and note that principle one's qualifier does real work: the data are incompatible with the null *and every other modelling assumption*, so a violated independence assumption produces small p-values on its own. **The ASA wrote this in 2016 because misuse had become widespread enough to distort published science**, which is a stronger statement than any textbook caveat.
